speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Good day.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: My second FOMC Committee meeting as Chairman has come quickly.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: It’s probably too early to call it a streak, but our discussions again were collegial and constructive.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: I’m truly lucky to work with colleagues so capable and mission focused, and so determined, like I am, to sharpen the performance of the Federal Reserve.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Today, as you know, our Committee decided to vote by a 9-to-3 vote to maintain the target range for the federal funds rate at 3½ to 3¾ percent.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: The Committee is continuing its policy of making ample reserves in the banking system.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: The economy is showing impressive resilience.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Even with recent shocks, the trends are positive and reveal solid growth.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Job gains have kept pace with the workforce, and the unemployment rate has changed little.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Inflation remains elevated relative to the Committee’s 2 percent goal.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: The Committee remains resolute.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: You’ve heard this before, but we will deliver price stability.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: As before, the policy statement conveys just the facts.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: It’s steering clear of forecasting, a choice we consider especially prudent at these uncertain times.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Uncertainty, however, does not mean a lack of clarity.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: For some households, businesses, and market professionals, five years of high inflation have left a mistaken impression that’s hard to shake—that the Fed’s implicit inflation target was somehow above 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Let me reiterate: There is no soft inflation target; there is no soft implicit target—not on this Committee’s watch.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: There’s only a target, and it’s 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Not one of my FOMC colleagues is under any illusion.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: We’ve begun a new chapter, and we understand that the five-plus years of inflation above target cannot be cured in nine weeks—or by a single month of modest price decreases.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: This Fed will not waver.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Our credibility rests on performing our duties and delivering on our responsibilities.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Americans are right to expect that because our nation’s prosperity depends on it.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: To the regulars here in the press room, today’s assessment might sound familiar.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Yet there was nothing inertial about our discussions, our policy, or our strategy.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Two economic developments are worth highlighting.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: The first is a very notable change since our last meeting 42 days ago: Nominal and real yields are materially higher across the Treasury curve.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: In fact, some of the increases in market interest rates between FOMC meetings are among the most significant in the last two decades, ranking around the top decile or so.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: But if the Committee didn’t change its policy rate, what happened?

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: In the intermeeting period, market attention centered on real data and real economic developments.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Prices reacted in real time to incoming information, and the reduction in forward guidance may have been a factor.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Market participants are learning to play the ball, not the referee—and market prices will continue to respond in the direction and magnitude they see fit.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: This is, in my view, a change for the better—and we’re just getting started.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: After all, the central bank need not always and everywhere be the center of attention.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: I understand the desire for rolling forecasts and commentary from this Committee.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: But for our part, we need to observe market reaction to developments, direct and unfiltered.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: I want to stress, of course, that decisions by this Committee matter a great deal.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: And where necessary and appropriate, we will not hesitate to act.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: A second economic development is one that I noted at the congressional oversight hearings this month, but it’s worth repeating.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: The most striking feature of the economy is the strong growth of business investment.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: The surge in high-tech capex has been remarkable.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: But that does not necessarily make the Fed’s role any easier.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: In the AI-related category of high-tech equipment and software, the most recent data shows four-quarter growth rates of nearly 20 percent.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: This is helping to sustain the healthy momentum of manufacturing output.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: More generally, capex is preparing the ground for future growth.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Nonetheless, the precise timing and magnitude of effects on the supply side remain hard to predict.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: FOMC meetings produce policy decisions.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: But just as important is candid discussion of the big things that matter most.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: That, too, is a priority in this new chapter at the Fed.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: In our meeting, vigorous discussion centered on four questions, which I will enumerate.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: First, we talked a lot about the implications of the past five years of high inflation on the current policy conjuncture.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: To, to echo an old phrase, has the past really passed?

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Second, my colleagues and I considered the economic shocks of recent years.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Strained supply chains arising from the pandemic, military conflicts, energy supply disruptions, substantial increases in tariff rates, and, yes, the surge in AI-related investment.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: These differ in their sources—do they also differ in their effects on output and employment?

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Third, we took up the related question of price increases arising from shocks.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: The business capex boom, for example, is driving up prices of memory and logic chips and associated AI infrastructure.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Do those changes indicate a broader inflationary dynamic, or do we just focus on them because they are under the bright streetlight?

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Finally, we discussed monetary policy tools and strategies for achieving stable prices.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: If, as the Fed has long held, interest rate policy should be its primary monetary policy instrument, how much accommodation are we getting from the balance sheet?

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: In all of this, our work is advancing at the Fed.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: We’re asking the right questions.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: And in this consequential time, we know how very much depends on getting the right answers.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Of course, you’ve all arrived with questions of your own, so let’s turn to them now.

speaker: MICHELLE SMITH
sentence: Let’s start with Steve.

speaker: STEVE LIESMAN
sentence: Thank you for taking our questions, Mr. Chairman.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Sure.

speaker: STEVE LIESMAN
sentence: You’ve had a couple months now, or nine weeks—whatever number it is—to see the markets behave in the absence of forward guidance.

speaker: STEVE LIESMAN
sentence: I’m wondering if you could tell me—what message are you getting from the markets as to where policy ought to be right now?

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Yeah, so I think officially it’s eight weeks and four days.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: But, I’m not counting.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: [Laughter] The message from markets is the message from markets.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: What I’ve really been trying to do, Steve, as I think you appreciate—and your colleagues appreciate—is getting an unfiltered message from markets.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Getting a direct message.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Letting buyers and sellers meet at prices for Treasuries—for the foreign exchange value of the dollar.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: And then trying to judge for ourselves—what does that mean about our remit?

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: How are we doing on inflation?

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: How are we doing on employment?

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: We’re trying not to interfere with that market signal.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: That’s part of the reason why we’ve been somewhat spare on our words when we pulled back from forward guidance.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: So they’re reacting to events, I would say, much more directly over the 42 days since we last met.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: This is a good thing.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: As I mentioned in the prepared remarks, we’ve seen a material tightening, not just in nominal rates, but in real rates, too, and we’re observing it.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: We’re trying to stay out of that because, you know, many of you might be interested in our reaction function—we’re interested in the reaction of financial markets.

speaker: STEVE LIESMAN
sentence: I—I get that, Mr. Chairman.

speaker: STEVE LIESMAN
sentence: And I guess the follow-up question is, if the markets are talking to you, what do you hear them saying?

speaker: STEVE LIESMAN
sentence: And if it’s “real rates are higher,” it would suggest that that’s where the funds rate ought to go.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Yeah, so— STEVE LIESMAN.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: And—sorry.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: I’m sorry—it’s your question.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: So interpreting markets is an imperfect business.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: We central bankers, like market pros, can think these things are overdetermined.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: But let me offer some speculation.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: First, as we said in the FOMC statement that you got at two o’clock, the economy—output is solid.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Capex and productivity are strong—labor markets—solid, steady.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: The bond market—the Treasury market—it seems to be saying that as well.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: If I were to try to break down—just aggregate the Treasury market signals—I wouldn’t be able to do it perfectly.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: But the bond market’s saying many of those same things, and that’s why we’re seeing a tightening both in nominals and in reals, even while, at some level, we haven’t done much in 42 days.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: The markets have done quite a bit.

speaker: MICHELLE SMITH
sentence: Claire.

speaker: CLAIRE JONES
sentence: Thank you.

speaker: CLAIRE JONES
sentence: Claire Jones, Financial Times.

speaker: CLAIRE JONES
sentence: You seem to have got the family fight you were after at this meeting.

speaker: CLAIRE JONES
sentence: [Laughter] We saw three—we saw three dissents.

speaker: CLAIRE JONES
sentence: Could you characterize the arguments that those dissenters put forward, please, and tell us a little bit why you weren’t persuaded by them at this stage?

speaker: CLAIRE JONES
sentence: Thank you.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: So I guess I shouldn’t give you their best arguments.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: I’ll give you some others.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: [Laughter] So you’re right.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: I asked for a good family fight, and I got one.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: That’s the purpose; that’s the design feature.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: I come into this meeting, even this press conference, heartened by what I’ve experienced the last two days.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Most of our discussion were on the big questions that matter to the conduct of monetary policy.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: We, we didn’t sort of hide from them—we weren’t scared of them.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: There was a lot more interaction between and among my colleagues.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: It was a real family fight.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: My view, which you’ve long heard, is that’s the better way to get policy right.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: That’s our North Star.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: So there was a lot of agreement that I heard—that we have the powers, the tools—also the authority to deliver stable prices.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: No walking back from our responsibilities—there was a large majority support for the decision that we made in the room, but I also want to leave you, Claire, with one other impression.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: There was nothing inertial about that discussion.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: It was an active, robust discussion about what’s in the full range of what we can do, and might want to do, in the period ahead.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: You characterized accurately—there was a disagreement about a decision today.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: I would say that doesn’t sort of capture the full essence of the discussion.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: The path to central bank heaven requires delivering on our remit.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: These days, that means delivering on price stability.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: I wouldn’t measure that path in 42 days—or any one particular meeting.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: And I came out of that meeting even more confident that this is the right team to win the battle against high inflation.

speaker: CLAIRE JONES
sentence: How much do you think not going in July was down to the cool CPI “print” for June?

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: So, in two words, not much—not much—I’d like to believe that the Committee shares my views, which is the historic problem with data dependence is the data and the dependence.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: We are not relying on any one individual piece of data as cover or as an excuse or as validation.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: What I care about, and what I think the Committee cares about, is trends on the data.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Sure, we got some encouraging inflation data.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: I think at the meeting 42 days ago I said something like “63 months of inflation above target.” I didn’t say “64,” though the final calculation might, might be a close one.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: So we’ll be—we’ll be watching inflation data over the period ahead, but I also don’t want you to leave the misimpression that we’re sort of breathlessly waiting that.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: I’ve called for a task force to revisit both the private and public data we use to make our decisionmaking.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: That task force is out doing their work.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: I’ll be checking back in with them in the next couple of weeks, but I wouldn’t say we overly relied on, on any one piece of data, including that data, which surprised some a couple of weeks ago.

speaker: MICHELLE SMITH
sentence: Neil.

speaker: NEIL IRWIN
sentence: Hi, Chairman Warsh, thanks.

speaker: NEIL IRWIN
sentence: Neil Irwin with Axios.

speaker: NEIL IRWIN
sentence: Thank you for taking our questions.

speaker: NEIL IRWIN
sentence: So the fed funds rate is now about 75 basis points below the two-year yield—suggests markets think you’ll have to tighten eventually—about 100 basis points below most Taylor rule estimates.

speaker: NEIL IRWIN
sentence: You’re hitting your employment mandate; inflation stays high.

speaker: NEIL IRWIN
sentence: Why should rates not be higher today?

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: There’s a lot in there, Neil.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: So rates are higher today than they were 42 days ago.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Markets have made decisions because we stepped back, in part, from trying to influence those.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Market judgments have moved up on what nominal rates are across the Treasury curve.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: That doesn’t mean we take them as—by dictation, but we’re observing them.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: So I think it’s a mischaracterization to say that markets haven’t reacted because we didn’t move today.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Markets are reacting in real time.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: In the period ahead, we’ve got important decisions to make about the policy rate.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Markets in the intervening period, I think, have quite a bit of decisions to make.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: I’ll see if I can put it this way: Monetary policy matters not just by what we say, or even what we do—monetary policy matters by how it affects the real economy.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: And these prices that we see in financial markets is one of the many ways in which it affects the real economy.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: We’ll be continuing to watch that market information—see how it responds to incoming events—and that can help inform our decisionmaking when we meet in seven or eight weeks.

speaker: NEIL IRWIN
sentence: How would you characterize, of the—in the family fight the last couple days—of you and the other eight members who wanted to hold?

speaker: NEIL IRWIN
sentence: Was that a strong conviction, or was that a hair-trigger close call on holding versus tightening?

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Well, I think, you know, the vote—the vote was 9 to 3.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: The broader discussion, to my ear, over the course of the last days showed a lot of agreement on the hard questions—the four questions I raised at the outset about what’s really happening in the economy with the shocks and absent the shocks.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: What are our tools and our capabilities?

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: What’s the effect on prices and on output?

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: I heard a lot of commonality on the questions.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Were there different “leans” on the answers?

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: You bet there was.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: So could people come to different conclusions?

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Absolutely.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: But my own judgment is this is a period of watchful thinking, not watchful waiting.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: And I think the score on that vote was unanimous.

speaker: MICHELLE SMITH
sentence: Colby.

speaker: COLBY SMITH
sentence: Thank you, Colby Smith with the New York Times.

speaker: COLBY SMITH
sentence: You’ve mentioned that looking at the Fed’s policy tools as one element of a three-pronged strategy to address the inflation problem.

speaker: COLBY SMITH
sentence: So I’m curious how you view the effectiveness of those tools.

speaker: COLBY SMITH
sentence: If inflation is too high and not coming down, is the best remedy to raise interest rates?

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: So that’s—that was the discussion the last two days.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Is that the dominant remedy?

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: If inflation continues to be elevated through the forecast period, interest rates could well be part of that solution.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: But I wouldn’t say it’s in isolation.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: I tried to describe in my remarks today the point that I made in—to the oversight committees a couple of weeks ago.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: I think there was a misimpression—by some in financial markets, by some households and businesses—that central bankers like me—we set a 2 percent inflation target, but maybe we were more tolerable of a somewhat higher inflation target.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: In economics, we’d call that the revealed preference.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: And so might it have been rational for people to think, “Well, their inflation target’s somewhat higher”?

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: The—what I heard in the last two days—what I’ve heard in eight and a half weeks is “no.” We will deliver the 2 percent inflation target.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: That is the Committee’s definition of price stability.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: So one way, absent the tools that you reference, to ensure that we get there is ensure that expectations are centered around the right number.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: And I think we’ve made some progress on that.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: I am not suggesting we’re done on that.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: It’s worth reiterating.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: And, ultimately, the business we’re in, Colby, is performance.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: We’re going to be judged by how we perform.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: And that’s what we intend to do with the inflation target—making clear expectations is one part of it.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Making sure we demonstrate we’re responsible for it—we’re not blaming is another—and our policy tools, like you referenced, is the third and equally consequential part.

speaker: COLBY SMITH
sentence: How are you factoring the fact that a large portion of the inflation overshoot is being caused by supply shocks—as it’s mentioned again in, in the statement—does that blunt the effectiveness of rate hikes in your view?

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: First, on the premise of your question, it was almost as if you were listening to our discussion in the last day and a half.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: A lot of our focus was on trying to understand and identify underlying inflation dynamics amid shocks.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: We take these shocks seriously.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: There’ve been a series of them that have been hitting this economy.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: We’re not looking through them and saying, “Oh, they don’t matter.” But we’re trying to understand is—to what extent are these shocks broadening in their effect—broadening in their impact on prices that are quite far removed from it?

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Our goal is to have growth that is broadening and inflation that is becoming more limited—more circumscribed.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: I’ll be the first to admit the shocks make this job and this policy conjuncture a little tougher.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: But that’s among the chief questions we’ve asked ourselves.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: And, around the room, people have different views on it.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: I tend to think, in the coming months, we’re going to refine that view and have a better judgment, and we’re going to have market prices trying to help inform it, too.

speaker: MICHELLE SMITH
sentence: Edward.

speaker: EDWARD LAWRENCE
sentence: Thank you, Mr. Chairman.

speaker: EDWARD LAWRENCE
sentence: Edward Lawrence from FOX Business.

speaker: EDWARD LAWRENCE
sentence: I guess I want to drill down maybe a little bit—what specifically in your mind would be the argument, then, for a pause today?

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: So I wouldn’t characterize what we did as anything like a pause.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: I would characterize what we did as a rigorous review of the economic situation.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: I would characterize what we did as a review of the big, hard questions.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: And I’d characterize it as a view of what our own homework is to try to resolve those questions in the period ahead.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: If you were to try to force a description that this was a pause, I would say financial market prices would take the other side of that.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Financial market prices in this intermeeting period—they didn’t pause.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: They reacted to the inflation data in one direction—strong economic growth in the other direction.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: And nominal and real rates went up.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Did the Fed take an explicit change in its policy rate today?

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: No.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: But I think that’s the beginning of the story, not the end of the story.

speaker: EDWARD LAWRENCE
sentence: And, and, if I could, I did want to ask—not forward guidance, but looking forward [laughter]—traditionally, a Federal Reserve Chairman uses the Jackson Hole summit as, as sort of a reset of monetary policy.

speaker: EDWARD LAWRENCE
sentence: How do you look at the speech that you’re going to make in August?

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: I look at it like a blank piece of paper right now.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: I, I have not begun consideration with the incredible team here what would go into that document.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: I think you characterized it correctly.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Historically, at least for my first tour of duty at the Fed, the more recent periods—it would be sort of a setting-up speech more often than not—of what was going to be happening in the fall.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: I haven’t made any judgments on that.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: But those are judgments we’ll have to come to.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: If I could, in the high mountain air in Jackson, Wyoming, I’d like to also frame the big questions.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: There is a tendency, especially with the proliferation of meetings and press conferences, to get caught up in the myopic: “Did you do this by a quarter, or do that?” Ultimately, whether we deliver on price stability matters some—the decisions we make in six- or seven- or eight-week periods.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: But they matter more—what are the big questions?

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: What’s really happening with productivity?

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: What’s really happening with demographics?

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: What’s really happening to the global economy amid the shocks?

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Haven’t made a decision whether it’s going to be a big-picture speech or whether it’s going to be a more traditional set up for all the action we’re going to have between September and December—I will tell you one other thing that I am doing between now and Jackson Hole—is I’m checking with those task forces.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: My first principle of establishing a task force is—find the best subject matter experts anywhere in the world and put them together—especially put them together with other people who might disagree with them.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: In the next couple weeks, I’m going to be doing a check back in—giving them time to sort of think hard about their agenda, their debate, their schedule, and when they might be ready for prime time.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: I’ll be doing a little bit of that checking, and that may or may not inform anything I have to say in Jackson.

speaker: MICHELLE SMITH
sentence: Nick.

speaker: NICK TIMIRAOS
sentence: Nick Timiraos, the Wall Street Journal.

speaker: NICK TIMIRAOS
sentence: Chairman Warsh, I want to follow up on Colby’s question about policy transmission.

speaker: NICK TIMIRAOS
sentence: You’ve said there’s no cruel choice between stable prices and full employment.

speaker: NICK TIMIRAOS
sentence: Rates bring inflation down by cooling demand.

speaker: NICK TIMIRAOS
sentence: It’s generally thought that can show up in the labor market.

speaker: NICK TIMIRAOS
sentence: If that’s not the channel you’re relying on, what is?

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Yeah, so let me go back to first principles, Nick.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: I don’t believe that either part of our mandate is generally at war with the other part.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: I do not believe that price stability and full employment is an either-or proposition.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: There have been policymakers over the last several generations who have thought that there is a strict tradeoff there.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: That isn’t my judgment.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: In fact, my judgment is, if and when we deliver on our remit, we’re going to be satisfying both prongs.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: We’re going to have price stability and full employment.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: And, in fact, if you want to do the most harm to the labor markets, you would run a period of high inflation that’s variable such that employers—businesses —wouldn’t really know what’s going on.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: So I think the two parts of our mandate are equally important.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: We have no legislative orphans here.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: I’ve been talking mostly about price stability because we’re doing pretty well, collectively, as a country—as policymakers—on the full-employment side.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: But we’re doing considerably less well on prices.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: That’s why we describe them as elevated, and that’s what’s taken most of our discussion.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: In terms of transmission mechanisms of monetary policy, I think different tools work through different transmission mechanisms.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: The interest rates work through lending channels and credit channels—maybe confidence channels and foreign exchange.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: The balance sheet probably works through some other channels, like signaling and portfolio balance.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: We’re keeping full abreast of all these tools and making policy.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: But if the suggestion is somehow we’re going to be fine-tuning aggregate demand so it catches supply, that’s not my mental model.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: I don’t think we’re great in the fine-tuning business.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: We’re trying to get supply and demand in broad order, but, really, what we’re doing as we sit here today at this press conference—is I think we’ve got a reasonable sense of what aggregate demand looks like in this economy.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: We’re inferring aggregate supply.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: We’re making a judgment about what productivity is.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: And, in some sense, there’s a race between supply and demand.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: And the surge in business capex in and around AI is making that calculation a little harder to judge, but in the period ahead, we’re going to be trying to judge just that.

speaker: NICK TIMIRAOS
sentence: And if I could ask, where exactly was the disagreement today?

speaker: NICK TIMIRAOS
sentence: Was it about the inflation forecast, or was it something more around the, the risks—the, the tactics?

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Yeah, so I’m going to let the—I’ll let the dissenters speak for themselves.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: The way I heard it over the last two days was overwhelming agreement on objectives and authority and commitment.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: I didn’t hear anybody walking away from it.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: The judgments as to how best to achieve the price stability—that was probably the question that we were trying to answer.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: What’s the best move?

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: What’s the best strategy?

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: What’s the best way to achieve it?

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: And a second question that was asked is, when do we need to make those harder calls?

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: When do we need to make those decisions?

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: And like I said to one of your colleagues, I was comforted that markets in the intermeeting period weren’t reacting to us—they weren’t reacting to dots or to speeches—they appeared more than ever to be reacting to real-time events.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: So they’re gauging themselves the—how restrictive the Treasury curve should be.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: And that, I think, has been a useful development.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: We don’t endorse any particular market move, but it also suggests we observe them with keen interest.

speaker: MICHELLE SMITH
sentence: Jonnelle.

speaker: JONNELLE MARTE
sentence: Jonnelle Marte with Bloomberg.

speaker: JONNELLE MARTE
sentence: Following up on that, there was more uncertainty in the markets about what the Fed would do at this meeting.

speaker: JONNELLE MARTE
sentence: To some extent you might think that’s what you want to see, but my question is about—is there a point at which you would not want to surprise the markets if they were pricing in something with higher certainty that was opposite of what you were intending to do?

speaker: JONNELLE MARTE
sentence: What are the risks that you see associated with that?

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Yeah, so it’s a good question.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Surprise is not the objective function.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Surprise is not what we’re solving for.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: We have a clear North Star.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: What we’re solving for is how to make the best decisions.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Almost everything else should be in service to that goal.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: By not spoon-feeding markets, by not previewing our decisions, by not sort of giving nudges and leans, my colleagues and I have found in the intermeeting period what we’re getting is the views from a very accomplished [group of] economists.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: That’s the internals of financial markets.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Instead of just repeating or echoing what we’re saying back to us, they’re giving us somewhat—not perfect—their own judgment.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: So surprises are not the objective.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: But, at the same time, I would say, we didn’t come into this meeting feeling constrained by the full range of alternatives we had in front of us.

speaker: JONNELLE MARTE
sentence: So some of your peers have continued to discuss how they think about policy decisions, and if you don’t offer your reaction function or your way of thinking about it, how concerned are you that you’re ceding control of the narrative?

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: So, not very concerned—that’s a short answer to the question.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: When some people that follow the Fed say, “Well, we don’t want your forecast—we don’t want your dot—we just want your reaction function,” part of me hears the—“What we really want is your forecast; what we really want is your dot.” In terms of reaction function, let me sort of disabuse people of a question that may or may not be real and be out there.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Any central banker, especially a central banker where the labor markets are more or less at equilibrium—any central banker, when he or she sees underlying inflation moving higher—he or she is more inclined to tighten policy.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Again, when you’ve achieved the other side of your mandate and you see underlying inflation falling, he’s more inclined to loosen policy.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: That’s my reaction function, and I don’t suspect it will cause people to not continue to pry for more because the truth is, for a very long time, in a lot of countries, coming out of the 2008 crisis, where in crisis mode we were purposely providing a lot of information—trying to provide a lot of assurance, trying to tell people exactly what we’re going to do, offering forward guidance with clarity—as if we’re tying our own hands behind our back.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Well, in crisis mode, that strikes me as a very prudent policy.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: But in more benign conditions, it strikes me as worth revisiting.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: But markets and market participants and reporters have learned to devour all that information, so I take seriously that the pullback of forward guidance requires some transition.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Reform isn’t easy, but our general judgment is going to help us make better decisions and, in so doing, satisfy our remit.

speaker: MICHELLE SMITH
sentence: Paul Wiseman.

speaker: PAUL WISEMAN
sentence: Thank you.

speaker: MICHELLE SMITH
sentence: It’s coming.

speaker: MICHELLE SMITH
sentence: There’s a mic coming.

speaker: PAUL WISEMAN
sentence: Thank you.

speaker: PAUL WISEMAN
sentence: When you talk about the 2 percent inflation target, what measure are you relying on?

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Yeah, so I’ll give two answers.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: First, let me give the proper, standard answer.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: The, the Federal Reserve every January outlines a statement of purposes and strategy, and in that strategy document, which I believe was dated January of this year, it describes a measure of PCE inflation as the—as the objective function there.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: I have enough of my—so that, that’s our number—we’re sticking with it.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Who knows, come after next January, what we might say about strategy.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: I suspect the task forces might, might have something to add.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: But I’ll say this: Some version of the Lucas critique, some version of Goodhart’s law, in economics should remind us that when we talk about measures of inflation or something else and we describe those measures as being consistent with our objectives, we might make them such that they’re not very good measures or very good objectives.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Broadly, if you said to me standing in front of you, “I abide fully by the strategy document—we’re going to deliver 2 percent inflation,” and not a whisper more—but to achieve that, I’m looking at a broader set of inflation data than PCE.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: So without sort of fully revealing my cards, I’m trying to understand, like my colleagues—what’s the underlying generalized change in prices that are happening in the economy?

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: It is not a perfect science.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: I might have said 42 days ago, “I’ve got a task force for that.” But we have a data project that’s trying to look and see whether we can’t separate the noise from the signal.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: And so if you would hear a message from me—yes, I care about what the PCE “prints” are.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: I care about what the contributions are from CPI and everything else.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: But my—my lens is broader than that, even though the remit is quite narrow.

speaker: MICHELLE SMITH
sentence: Mike McKee.

speaker: MICHAEL MCKEE
sentence: Michael McKee from Bloomberg Radio and Television.

speaker: MICHAEL MCKEE
sentence: I’m struggling a little bit with some of what you’ve said today, and maybe you can help clarify this.

speaker: MICHAEL MCKEE
sentence: You’ve said over and over again that your job is to bring down prices—to get prices stable—to hit your target and that you will hit your target.

speaker: MICHAEL MCKEE
sentence: The market says you’re not there yet because they’ve raised rates.

speaker: MICHAEL MCKEE
sentence: But all you’ve talked about today is talking about it, and it’s not like members of the Committee weren’t there before you talking about it.

speaker: MICHAEL MCKEE
sentence: So I guess what the American people might be asking is, what are you waiting for?

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Yeah.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: So, believe it or not, this press conference is not all I’ve done today.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: We have spent an inordinate amount of time in the last two—two days—two weeks looking at our monetary policy strategy, evaluating our tools—thinking hard about the sources of data that we have at our disposal and we wish we had.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: We’ve also thought hard about the period ahead.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: What among these questions will be answered with more clarity?

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Certainly not certainty—so the decision we made today—the discussion we had in that room was the farthest thing from inertia I can imagine.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: As a point estimate at this very moment, in a choice between two alternatives, you heard the results of it, but I would tell you that this discussion was far more robust.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: And our thinking about how best to achieve that target is advanced, and over the coming months I expect it to be advanced much more significantly.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: If you were to sort of—if I were to steal a follow-up question, I won’t let you—you won’t be giving it up.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: If I were to steal a follow-up question, “Well, what’s—what’s the world think about what you’ve done?” I would again reiterate what we do isn’t just about what we say—it’s not just about what we do—we’re in the performance business.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: And so, so if I look at the Treasury curve, if I look at the dollar, if I look at a lot of things that are internals inside of financial markets, I think what they’re broadly saying is that this Committee does own it—has the credibility to deliver it.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: And they believe, like I do, that we will.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: But I don’t want to leave you with a misimpression—we’ve got no magic wand.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: This isn’t something that we’re going to be able to carry out in days or weeks.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: But we’re going to deliver on the responsibility that Congress gave us, and today’s meeting—and the preparation for today’s meeting—was an important step towards that destination.

speaker: MICHAEL MCKEE
sentence: I’d like to follow up on the task forces as well and ask—what vetting did you do of the people that you appointed to the task forces?

speaker: MICHAEL MCKEE
sentence: In particular, given Marc Andreessen’s substantial political spending—$25 million in just the past year to back candidates who oppose stricter I—AI regulation—how can the public be confident that a committee he co-chairs will provide an independent assessment of AI’s economic effects, rather than one aligned with the interests of the AI industry?

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Yeah, so I selected 15 incredible subject market—subject matter experts to tackle five of the most important questions that, if we get the answers right, we’re going to do a far better job in delivering.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: And if we get the answers wrong, we have a problem.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: The comfort that I can give you and your listeners is, we’re the decisionmakers.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: The Chairman of the Board of the Federal Reserve and the members of the Board and the FOMC—we will be the consumers of the outputs from five different committees.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: The judgments we’re making will be informed by—but not at all determined by—these outside groups.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: My theory of the case in establishing the task forces were to pick people with extraordinary talent, depth of expertise, and a divergence of views inside every committee so they, too, can have a family fight.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: This is not outsourcing to people that aren’t known and haven’t been vetted—this is seeing whether new ideas can catalyze a broader, better, more-informed discussion inside the room.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: And I’m very confident that we’re going to be able to do that.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: I am impressed by the credentials of these 15 people.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: And, full disclosure, I’ve known almost all of them for a very long time, and I think they’re going to give their best views on the subject.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: But, ultimately, these are decisions we’re going to make, and we’re accountable to our oversight committees and to the remit Congress gave us to deliver.

speaker: MICHELLE SMITH
sentence: Ann.

speaker: ANN SAPHIR
sentence: Hi, Ann Saphir with Reuters.

speaker: ANN SAPHIR
sentence: Nice to see you again—so I need a little help here, too.

speaker: ANN SAPHIR
sentence: You’ve—you’ve said repeatedly you have no tolerance for inflation.

speaker: ANN SAPHIR
sentence: And yet we are seeing above-target inflation repeatedly for five years and through your term so far.

speaker: ANN SAPHIR
sentence: And sure, you have no magic wand, but you have not taken action.

speaker: ANN SAPHIR
sentence: You just gave us a little peek at your reaction function as well.

speaker: ANN SAPHIR
sentence: You said that, if underlying inflation is rising, that you would tend to think that you might need to tighten.

speaker: ANN SAPHIR
sentence: And, with the exception of the most recent inflation “print,” that is what we’ve been seeing.

speaker: ANN SAPHIR
sentence: So could you explain what you mean by “no tolerance for inflation” and what you plan to do about it?

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Sure.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: So, Ann, I hear from you what I hear more broadly from households and businesses: impatience.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: “Deliver it already.” This is not a—this is not an excuse.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: This is a fact—this FOMC—this Board has been in business for eight and a half weeks.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: This—the, the patience—the impatience that households and businesses feel have been going on for 63 months.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: We are on the job; we will deliver.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: We are focused like a laser on making sure we can do it.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: But the suggestion that we’re going to be able to do it with our magic wand is one I want to disabuse you and everyone else of.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: But the discussion in the last two days give me more confidence, even than I had eight and a half weeks ago.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: This team that we have at the FOMC, the support that we have from Board staff, and the new hard questions we’re asking—we need to resolve those and, as we resolve those questions, get smarter on those.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: We’re going to deliver on the remit.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: You don’t have to take my word for it.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: If you look broadly at market prices, they are certainly not saying “all clear,” but they are working in concert to, to keep us on our toes, and they have tightened financial conditions in this intermeeting period.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: And, and that has given us a—that has provided us some—some comfort that, that we’ve got the ability and capability to deliver.

speaker: ANN SAPHIR
sentence: And, and is your read, or your, I guess, faith in markets’ ability to sort of make a judgment and then you to take signal from that judgment—is that—how does that affect you when you come up on the September meeting and markets are seeing a near 100 percent chance of a rate hike, as they see now?

speaker: ANN SAPHIR
sentence: How does that feed into your decisionmaking and your thinking?

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: So we’re not going to be constrained by market prices.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: We’re not going to be constrained or take verbatim from what the market’s doing.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: But I think it’s useful, Ann, to understand that markets can be a very good source of information—not a determinative source—not a perfect source.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: But if we’re trying to land the plane and deliver 2 percent inflation and we take a very useful source of information and we get it all fogged up by giving it our own forecast—by providing rolling commentary—I can assure you that we’re going to have less information—less ability to land the plane successfully and deliver price stability.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: We’re just trying to make sure that that source of information is as direct and unfiltered as possible.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: It isn’t to the exclusion of data sources and opinions and other surveys, but if you’re hearing from me, we wanted to make sure we’re getting a better source of information.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: I think, in a relatively short time, we are.

speaker: MICHELLE SMITH
sentence: We’ll go to Brian Cheung for the last question.

speaker: BRIAN CHEUNG
sentence: Hi there, Chairman Warsh.

speaker: BRIAN CHEUNG
sentence: Brian Cheung with NBC News.

speaker: BRIAN CHEUNG
sentence: So you said you’d be open to having press conferences when there’s news to make.

speaker: BRIAN CHEUNG
sentence: So, today, no change to rates, no forward guidance—for the average household, I guess, what was the news today?

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: So, apparently, it was news that I had a press conference.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Let me just see if I can offer some clarity on that.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Between now and year-end, my predecessors and the Federal Reserve committed to press conferences this year.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: I’m committing to press conferences this year.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: That might be news to the people in this room, and of no particular interest to your viewers and your—[laughter]—and your readers back at home.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: What I can offer as assurance is that the Fed’s on the case—that this Fed Chairman feels better about this Board and this Committee’s ability to deliver than I did when I showed up here on the first day.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: And I showed up pretty confident.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: I’ve been heartened by the reception that I received.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: No doubt in some of your commentaries today you’ll talk about a divided Federal Reserve, but that’s not the feeling I felt the last couple of days and the couple days before it.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: What I felt was a group of professionals—all the different perspectives, different views, different judgments—but eager to roll up their sleeves and have a family fight and eager to reform the way in which the Fed does policy—a keenness and open-mindedness and curiosity about that.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: So we have a far better chance to deliver on the remit that Congress gave us, and so I want to leave you with the optimism of a new central banker that we’re committed as ever to deliver and to offer an assurance we will.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Thank you all very much.
